[[File:James Porter by WW Ouless.jpg|thumb|James Porter by [[Walter William Ouless]]]]
'''James Porter''' (2 October 1827, [[Belfast]] – 2 October 1900, [[Cambridge]])<ref>''The Master Of Peterhouse'' [[The Times]] (London, England), Wednesday,  Oct 03, 1900; pg. 4; Issue 36263</ref> was a British academic<ref>[http://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/c/F62858 National Archives]</ref> in the second half of the 19th century.<ref>{{Who's Who | title=Porter, James | id = U195346 | type = was | volume = 1897–1916 | edition = 1 December 2007 online | access-date = 1 August 2018 }}</ref>

Porter was born on 2 October 1827 in Belfast, the son of Rev. James Porter, Presbyterian minister, Rector of Drumlee, [[Castlewellan]], [[County Down]].<ref name="alum-cantab">{{acad|id=PRTR847J|name=Porter, James}}</ref> Porter's siblings were:
* [[William Archer Porter]], a [[lawyer]] and [[educationist]] who served as the principal of [[Government Arts College, Kumbakonam]] and tutor and secretary to the Maharaja of [[Mysore kingdom|Mysore]];
* Jane Bailie Porter, who married [[Alexander Crum Brown]], the Scottish organic chemist;
* Margaret Archer Porter, who married [[Peter Guthrie Tait]], the physicist.

Porter graduated [[Master of Arts (Scotland)|M.A.]] from the [[University of Glasgow]] in 1847, and continued to [[Peterhouse, Cambridge]] (admitted 8 July 1847, graduated [[Bachelor of Arts|B.A.]] as [[Wrangler (University of Cambridge)|9th wrangler]] 1851, [[Master of Arts (Oxford, Cambridge, and Dublin)|M.A.]] 1854, [[Doctor of Divinity|D.D.]] 1881).<ref name="alum-cantab"/>

Porter taught mathematics at [[Liverpool College]]<ref>[https://www.lookandlearn.com/history-images/U275305/The-late-Reverend-James-Porter-DD-Master-of-Peterhouse-Cambridge Look & Learn]</ref> 1851–55, and was ordained deacon in 1853 and priest in 1856.<ref name="alum-cantab"/>

He was to spend the rest of his career at Peterhouse. He was appointed [[Fellow]] in 1853; [[Dean (education)|Dean]] in 1856; [[Bursar]] in 1861; Assistant Tutor in 1863; [[Tutor]] 1866–76; and Master 1876–1900. He also served as [[Senior proctor]] in 1868–69 and 1876–77; [[Vicar]] of [[Cherry Hinton]] 1880–82;<ref name="alum-cantab"/> and [[Vice-Chancellor of the University of Cambridge]] 1881–84.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.v-c.admin.cam.ac.uk/role-vice-chancellor/history-vice-chancellorship |title=University web-site |access-date=1 August 2018 |archive-date=3 April 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190403203920/https://www.v-c.admin.cam.ac.uk/role-vice-chancellor/history-vice-chancellorship |url-status=dead }}</ref>

"He was endowed with a great activity both mental and physical, which found expression on the one hand in a keen participation in athletic sports, and on the other in whole-hearted efforts to promote the highest interests of the University."<ref>{{cite book |last=Knott |first=Cargill Gilston |date=1911 |title=Life and Scientific Work of Peter Guthrie Tait |url=https://archive.org/stream/cu31924064123148#page/n33 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |page=14 |author-link=Cargill Gilston Knott}}</ref> In Dr T. A. Walker's History of Peterhouse (1906) the Rev. James Porter is described as a “man of notable business qualifications and of a rare generosity of spirit.”<ref>{{cite book |last=Walker |first=Thomas Alfred |date=1906 |title=Peterhouse |url=https://archive.org/stream/peterhouse00walkgoog#page/n210/search/James+Porter |location=London |publisher=Hutchinson & Co |page=187}}</ref>
